# load-lock: machine-wide heavy-work coordination

All coding agents on this machine (any harness, any repo/worktree) share one
small budget of heavy-work permits. Before resource-intensive local work, a
polite agent acquires a permit; everyone else keeps doing light work until an
offer arrives.

## How to call load-lock

Use the first of these that works; they all talk to the same daemon:

1. **load-lock MCP tools** (`acquire`, `wait_for_turn`, `run_with_permit`,
   ...), if your harness lists them. The rest of this skill names them.
2. **`load-lock` on PATH**: check with `load-lock version`.
3. **Pinned npx**: `npx -y @aron98/load-lock@1.7.1 <command>` (Node >= 20).
   It downloads that exact npm package once into the npx cache. Below,
   read `load-lock` as this whole prefix. `npm install -g @aron98/load-lock`
   makes it permanent.

The first call starts the daemon on its own (shared state in
`~/.local/state/load-lock`, or `$XDG_STATE_HOME/load-lock`); you never start
it yourself.

### CLI-only use (no MCP tools)

`load-lock help` lists every command. The safest flow is `load-lock run`,
which acquires a permit, runs the command, and releases it when the command
exits (success or failure):

```sh
load-lock run --reason "full test suite" --op-key test/all -- npm test
```

- Exit code **68** with `queued at position N (request <id>)` means you are
  not allowed to start yet. Keep doing light work. Out of light work? Sleep
  honestly with `load-lock wait --id <request-id> --timeout 600000`: it
  wakes you on your turn, claims the offer, and prints a `permit_token`.
  Then `load-lock run --permit <permit_token> -- npm test`. A `wait` that
  exits 68 again (still queued) is a checkpoint: call it again.
- No longer need a queued request: `load-lock cancel --id <request-id>`.
  Your own offers, queue entries and paused requests: `load-lock pending`.

**Identity.** The daemon routes offers and `pending` per agent. The CLI
derives your agent id from your harness session (Claude Code and OpenCode
session env vars; on Linux, otherwise your harness process), so every call
from one session counts as one agent, and other sessions are other agents.
If `pending` does not show a request you made, pin the id yourself: set
`LOAD_LOCK_AGENT=<unique-name>` (or pass `--agent <unique-name>`) on every
call.

Skill-only use has no idle wakeup (nothing tells you an offer arrived while
you sit idle; use `load-lock wait`) and no policy reminder after context
compaction. To get both, install the harness integration once:
`load-lock setup` (or `load-lock install --harness <name>`).

## When to use it

**Heavy** (acquire first): full builds, `cargo build`/`npm run build`, whole
test suites, codegen over the whole repo, bulk compilation, anything that
pins several cores or gobs of RAM for minutes.

**Light** (no permit): file edits, greps, small targeted tests, single-file
checks, reading, planning, git operations, anything sub-second or trivial.

Judge by *expected* CPU/memory/IO impact, not by command name. When unsure,
`inspect_machine` shows real capacity (incl. container limits) and pressure.

## Core flow

1. `acquire(reason, op_key)` — idempotent per `op_key`. Result is either
   `granted` (you hold a permit; start heavy work now) or `queued`
   (keep doing light work; an offer will arrive).
2. While queued: **continue useful light work**. Do not idle-poll.
   Out of light work? `wait_for_turn(request_id?, timeout_ms?)` — a
   bounded blocking sleep until your turn that auto-claims the offer and
   wakes you with the permit_token (holds no capacity; cancellation
   leaves nothing behind).
3. When an offer arrives (harness wakeup or `pending`): `claim(offer_token)`
   inside the claim window (default 30s). Expired offers are rejected; your
   request pauses until you `rejoin`.
4. Only after `granted`/`claim` succeeds, start the heavy work. Associate the
   work with the permit:
   - `run_with_permit(permit_token, command)` — best: spawns it, tracks the
     process group, auto-releases on exit. Poll `job_status`; do NOT release
     manually.
   - `attach_pid(permit_token, pid)` — for a process you already started
     (e.g. a background shell task). Auto-release when it exits.
   - `mark_started(permit_token)` — last resort, no process association
     (heartbeat lease applies instead).
5. `release(permit_token)` when done (idempotent), or `cancel(request_id)`
   for queue entries you no longer need. Background jobs that outlive your
   session keep their permit until the *process* exits — never release just
   because a tool call returned a background-task id.

## Cleanup rules (why you still see permits released)

- Offers expire (short window) and never auto-recycle: a missed offer pauses
  your request; `rejoin(request_id)` puts you back in the FIFO queue.
- Claimed-but-never-started permits are reclaimed at the start deadline
  (default 120s) so a forgotten claim can't block the queue.
- Tracked jobs (run_with_permit/attach_pid) hold the permit exactly as long
  as the process (group) lives; completion/failure releases automatically.
- Untracked (mark_started) permits are held under a heartbeat lease — if your
  harness adapter disappears without a trace of the work, the lease reclaims
  the permit. The tradeoff: a still-running but unobserved process could
  overlap with new work. Prefer tracking.
- Never auto-released merely for being held a long time, if the work is
  confirmed running.

## Machine awareness and config

- `inspect_machine` — cores, memory, cgroup/container limits, current pressure.
- `get_config` / `configure(expected_version, changes, reason)` — compare-and-swap
  capacity and timing changes; read the version first, always explain why.
- `status` — machine-wide snapshot: holders, offers, queue.
- Anyone may adjust the budget; changes are persisted with rationale+author.

## Recovery

- `pending` — your own offers/queue/holds (check before giving up).
- `load-lock status` / `load-lock recover list` (human CLI) shows orphaned
  permits with process liveness; `load-lock recover force-release --id` is the
  explicit escape hatch (it prints holder/job info first).
- Daemon restart: running tracked permits survive (journaled); queued/offered
  requests do not — re-`acquire`.

**A machine-wide heavy-work budget for parallel coding agents.** When several agents work side by side on one machine — separate sessions, repos, git worktrees, or harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code, ...) — their builds and test suites stomp on each other, thrash the caches, and starve each other's cores. load-lock gives them one shared counting semaphore: acquire a permit before heavy work, keep doing light work while queued, receive a FIFO offer when capacity frees, claim it, run, release. It is cooperative and advisory — no command wrapping, no automatic shell classification, no approval interruptions. ``` agent A (OpenCode) agent B (Codex) agent C (Claude Code) acquire "cargo test" acquire "npm test" acquire "build docs" granted ✓ runs queued → keeps coding queued → keeps coding ... offer → claim ✓ runs (misses window → paused) release ✓ release ✓ rejoin → offer → claim ✓ ``` Three agents, one budget — the queue drains FIFO while everyone keeps coding:

## Features - **One budget for the whole machine** — every client of any harness shares one capacity pool regardless of repo/worktree/cwd. Default: pool `heavy`, capacity 1; fully runtime-configurable by any agent via versioned CAS updates (persisted with author + rationale). - **Atomic acquire-or-queue** — single daemon event loop; a release can never slip between a failed check and queue registration. - **FIFO offers with opaque claim tokens** — outstanding offers reserve capacity; expired offers pass capacity to the next waiter and pause the absent request until it explicitly rejoins (no endless recycling). - **Real process-lifecycle cleanup** — permits attach to actual processes (pid + process group + `/proc` start time, PID-reuse-safe). Background jobs outliving the shell keep their permit until the whole group exits. Never auto-expired merely for being old. Untracked work uses an honest, documented heartbeat-lease tradeoff. Explicit release is always available and idempotent. - **Crash-safe** — agent crashes release tracked permits on confirmed process death; daemon restarts reconcile a journal against real liveness and auto-respawn transparently. - **Honest notifications** — tool-boundary offer delivery everywhere; real idle wakeup where the harness supports it (live-verified on OpenCode; hook-based on Claude Code and Codex CLI); a bounded blocking `wait_for_turn` (`load-lock wait` on the CLI) that sleeps until your turn and auto-claims for harnesses without idle wakeup; durable event ids for reconnects. A notification never authorizes work — only `claim` does. - **Policy that actually reaches the model** — installed per harness via its real mechanism (plugin context hook, SessionStart hooks incl. compact matchers, global instruction files), plus a detailed skill/guide. - **Resource-aware** — `inspect_machine` reports cgroup/container CPU and memory limits and current pressure; never assumes cores = capacity. ## Install Pick a rung per harness. # Writing a harness adapter for load-lock

load-lock ships first-class support for OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex CLI,
plus a generic MCP fallback that works with any MCP-capable harness. This
guide is for anyone adding support for a *new* harness. Everything you need
is importable from the published package — no private APIs required.

```ts
import { LLClient, withClient } from "@aron98/load-lock/shared/client";
import type * as P from "@aron98/load-lock/shared/protocol";
import { POLICY_BRIEF } from "@aron98/load-lock/policy/text";
import { buildServer } from "@aron98/load-lock/mcp/server";
```

## What a good adapter provides (in priority order)

1. **Tools** — the agent must be able to call acquire / claim / release /
   cancel / pending / status / inspect_machine / get_config / configure, and
   ideally the lifecycle helpers (run_with_permit / job_status / attach_pid /
   mark_started).
2. **Policy at session start** — inject `POLICY_BRIEF` where the harness
   puts per-session instructions, and re-inject after context compaction if
   the harness supports it. This is the part agents actually follow; tools
   without teaching get ignored.
3. **Idle wakeup (if the harness allows it)** — when the daemon emits an
   `offered` event for your session, deliver it to the agent at a safe
   point (execution boundary), including the claim token and expiry. Never
   interrupt an in-flight tool call.
4. **Heartbeats** — every ~30s while the session is alive, so
   `mark_started` (untracked) permits aren't reclaimed while the agent is
   merely quiet.

Pick the tier your harness allows:

## Tier 1 — native plugin (best)

For harnesses with an in-process extension API (this is what the OpenCode
adapter does — see `src/adapters/opencode/plugin.ts` as the worked example):

- One module-level `LLClient` (it auto-spawns the daemon on first use; a
  machine typically runs one client per plugin host).
- Register tools that translate your harness's tool-call format into
  `client.request(...)`. Give the agent a stable identity (harness session
  id) and pass the session's cwd at acquire time.
- Subscribe `client.watch("*")` and route `offered` events to the owning
  session via the harness's wake/synthetic-message API.
- Inject `POLICY_BRIEF` on session start and after every compaction.
- For heavy work, implement a `run_with_permit` helper following the
  lifecycle contract below — or teach agents to use the CLI
  (`load-lock run --permit ... -- <cmd>`), which already implements it.

## Tier 2 — hooks + MCP

For harnesses with lifecycle hooks but no in-process API (Claude Code and
Codex CLI use this): keep the stock MCP server (`load-lock-mcp` binary,
`load-lock mcp`, or `node .../dist/mcp/main.js`) for tools, and add hook handlers that shell out
to the CLI:

- `load-lock hook <harness> session-start` → prints `POLICY_BRIEF` +
  machine summary for context injection (register for post-compaction too,
  if the harness has a compact matcher).
- `load-lock hook <harness> stop` → checks cwd-matched offers and, if one
  exists, prints the harness's "continue the session" JSON with the claim
  token. Honors any stop-loop flags the harness provides.
- See `src/cli/hook.ts` for the implementation pattern and
  `src/cli/install.ts` for the config-writing/installer pattern.

## Tier 3 — MCP only

Register the MCP server with the harness and put a short policy section in
whatever global instructions file the harness reads (GEMINI.md / rules /
hints...). Offers are surfaced in every tool result (tool-boundary
delivery), so correctness is preserved; what you lose is idle wakeup —
steer agents to `wait_for_turn` (bounded blocking sleep that auto-claims
and returns a `permit_token`) as the primary idle mechanism, and to
`wait_for_completion` (bounded execution-phase sleep) once a job runs.
Document the remaining gap honestly (see docs/COMPATIBILITY.md).

## Shipped adapter: Hermes Agent (plugins/hermes)

The Hermes plugin is a hybrid: **tier-1-style native plugin** (tools, hooks,
slash command, skill, dashboard tab registered in-process) with **tier-2
transport** (each tool shells out to the local `load-lock` CLI in `--json`
mode instead of speaking the socket protocol from Python). Rationale: one
runtime to keep honest (the CLI already implements the lifecycle contract,
exit-code conventions, and `run`), zero Python dependencies, and the same
daemon either way.

What it registers:

- 19 `load_lock_*` tools (full MCP surface minus `agent_guide`, which ships
  as the bundled `load-lock:agent-guide` skill), wrapping the CLI with
  `--agent hermes:<session_id>` derived from handler kwargs. CLI exit codes
  (68 queued / 69 wait-resolution) map into structured JSON results — tools
  never raise.
- A local Python job registry for `run_with_permit` mirroring the MCP
  server's semantics: spawn via `load-lock run --permit ... -- <cmd>`,
  output ring buffer, watcher/reaper threads, auto-release on exit,
  `job_status` / `job_stop` / `wait_for_completion(job_id)`.
- `pre_llm_call` hook injecting `POLICY_BRIEF` on the first turn and
  re-injecting after compaction (the `post_compaction` hook on 0.23+,
  with a shrinking-history heuristic as the fallback for older builds),
  plus a best-effort machine status line.
- `on_session_end` cancelling the session's queued requests, and a
  background heartbeat thread (interval ≈ `untracked_lease_ms / 3`) so
  untracked permits of live-but-quiet sessions aren't reclaimed.
- `pre_tool_call` giving `run_with_permit` the `terminal` tool's
  dangerous-command gate: a command Hermes's detector flags is escalated
  to the human-approval gate via the `approve` directive.
- A read-only dashboard tab (`dashboard/`): API routes shell out to
  `status` / `inspect` / `events --since`, the frontend polls them.
- A desktop half (`desktop/plugin.js`, Hermes Desktop 0.23+): a Load Lock
  tiling pane on the workspace's right edge, an `LL used/total` status-bar
  chip colored by pressure, and a command-palette row — all fed by the
  same routes through `ctx.rest`. Polling (2s) stays the source of truth;
  the backend additionally tails `events --follow` and broadcasts
  `plugin.load-lock.state.changed` (0.23+ plugin events) so an attached
  Desktop invalidates instantly.

Runtime resolution mirrors `plugins/claude-code/scripts/load-lock.mjs`:
`load_lock_command` setting → `load-lock` on PATH (version-checked) →
newest state-dir copy → optional pinned `npx` fallback (`auto_install`,
off by default).

Known gap, documented honestly: Hermes has no idle-wakeup/synthetic
message hook, so offers are surfaced tool-boundary only (every result
embeds `pending`) and agents are steered to `wait_for_turn` — the same
baseline as tier 3. `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` labels it live-verified
against Hermes 0.23.0 (agent tools also verified on 0.19.0).

## Protocol quick reference

Wire protocol: NDJSON over a Unix domain socket (named pipe on Windows);
`LLClient` handles
framing, timeouts, auto-spawn, and event subscriptions. Methods an adapter
normally touches:

| Method | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `acquire {pool?, agentId, agentLabel?, labelPrefix?, cwd?, opKey, reason, weight?, waitMs?, subscribeIfBusy?}` | grant / queue (idempotent per agent+opKey); labelPrefix composes `prefix:label` holder labels for sandboxed clients (env `LOAD_LOCK_LABEL_PREFIX` is injected by the shared client) |
| `claim {offerToken}` | offer → permit (before starting heavy work) |
| `release {permitToken, outcome?}` | idempotent |
| `cancel {requestId}` / `rejoin {requestId}` / `decline {offerToken}` | queue hygiene |
| `pending {agentId}` | the caller's offers/queue/holds (attach to every tool result) |
| `status {pool?}` / `inspect` / `get_config` / `configure {expectedVersion, changes, reason, author}` | state + versioned CAS config |
| `start_job {permitToken, pid, pgid?}` | atomic permit↔process association (tracked) |
| `mark_started {permitToken}` | untracked lease fallback |
| `heartbeat {agentId}` | keep untracked leases alive |
| `watch {agentId\|*}` / `events {sinceEventId, agentId?}` | push/pull event streams (durable ids) |
| `offers_for_cwd {cwd}` | for hook scripts without session identity |
| `hook_once {harness, sessionId, event, occurrence?, ttlMs?, hold?}` | hook dedupe: `{first}` is true only for the first caller per key; keys expire (TTL, default 60s) or, with `hold`, live as long as the connection; in-memory only |

## Lifecycle contract (the part that must not be improvised)

- Associate a permit with real execution **atomically**: spawn the job in
  its own process group, then `start_job` with pid+pgid; if association
  fails, kill the group immediately. Register exit listeners *before*
  awaiting the association RPC (a fast-exiting job can otherwise lose its
  release event — this was a real bug here).
- Never release because the shell returned a background-task id; release
  (or auto-release) on actual process-group completion.
- Do not auto-release on agent disconnect; that's the whole point of the
  daemon holding ownership.
- Untracked (`mark_started`) permits are only as good as your heartbeats;
  document the tradeoff and steer agents toward tracked paths.

## Testing your adapter

Reuse `src/test/testutil.ts`-style harness spawning (isolated
`LOAD_LOCK_STATE_DIR`/`LOAD_LOCK_SOCKET`, probe the socket, then
`LLClient`), or simply script against the CLI. Concurrency rules to verify:
capacity is never exceeded by held+offered, FIFO order holds, duplicate
acquires are idempotent, and a daemon restart keeps tracked permits
alive. Label your adapter honestly in docs/COMPATIBILITY.md:
implemented / contract-tested / live-verified.

# load-lock agent guide

load-lock coordinates heavy work across all coding agents on this machine.
Every session — any harness, any repo, any worktree — shares one machine-
wide capacity budget. Before resource-intensive work, acquire a permit. The
whole thing is cooperative: you decide what is heavy; the budget only works
if everyone participates.

This guide is also available as the `agent_guide` MCP tool, as
`load-lock agent-guide`, and as a skill in supported harnesses.

## 0. How to reach load-lock

Use the first of these that works; they all talk to the same daemon:

1. **load-lock tools** in your harness (MCP tools, or `load_lock_*` in
   OpenCode). The rest of this guide names the tools.
2. **`load-lock` on PATH** (check with `load-lock version`).
3. **Pinned npx**: `npx -y @aron98/load-lock@<version> <command>`, with the
   version the load-lock skill pins (Node >= 20). Read `load-lock` below as
   this whole prefix.

The first call starts the shared daemon; you never start it yourself.

**CLI only (skill-only install, no tools).** Prefer `load-lock run`: it
acquires, runs the command, and releases when it exits, success or failure:

```sh
load-lock run --reason "full test suite" --op-key test/all -- npm test
```

Exit code **68** means "not granted yet" (queued, with the request id in
the message): don't start the work. Keep doing light work; when you run out,
`load-lock wait --id <request-id>` sleeps until your turn, claims the offer
and prints a `permit_token` for `load-lock run --permit <permit_token> -- <cmd>`.
A `wait` that exits 68 again is a checkpoint: call it again. Your own
requests and offers: `load-lock pending`.

Your agent id is derived from your harness session, so all calls from one
session count as one agent. If `pending` doesn't show a request you made,
pin the id yourself with `LOAD_LOCK_AGENT=<unique-name>` (or `--agent`) on
every call. Without tools nothing wakes you while you sit idle and nothing
re-teaches the policy after context compaction; `load-lock setup` shows how
to add the harness integration that does.

## 1. Deciding heavy vs light

Judge by **expected** CPU/memory/IO cost, not by name:

- **Heavy** (acquire first): builds, test suites, `cargo build`/`cargo
  test`, `npm test`, container builds, migration runs, anything you expect
  to saturate cores or memory for more than a few seconds.
- **Light** (no permit): file edits, greps, reads, git status/diff, short
  shell snippets, install/status probes, anything bounded and cheap.

If in doubt about the machine's headroom, call `inspect_machine` — it
reports effective cores and memory *including container/cgroup limits*
(the machine may have 8 logical cores but a 2-core cgroup quota — never
assume "N cores means N jobs") plus current load and memory pressure. Use
`get_config`/`configure` when the budget genuinely needs adjustment.

## 2. Core flow

```
acquire(reason, op_key)
  ├─ granted  → you hold a permit → do the heavy work now
  ├─ queued   → keep doing LIGHT work; offers reach you at your next
  │             load-lock tool call, or via a wakeup message
  │             no light work left? wait_for_turn() = "sleep until it
  │             is my turn" (bounded; auto-claims the offer for you)
  └─ ...
offer arrives (token, expiry) → claim(token) BEFORE the window closes
claim → held → start the heavy work
  best:  run_with_permit(permit_token, command)   # daemon tracks the process
  else:  attach_pid(permit_token, pid)            # you started it yourself
  else:  mark_started(permit_token)               # lease-based, weaker
work finishes → release(permit_token)
no longer needed while queued → cancel(request_id)
offer arrived but you won't make it → decline(offer_token)
```

Rules, in order of importance:

1. **Acquire immediately before** the heavy work — not at the start of a
   long task.
2. **While queued, continue useful light work** — read code, write plans,
   make edits. Do not sleep or spin; offers are delivered to you.
3. **Claim before starting.** Heavy work starts only after `acquire`
   returned granted (or `claim` succeeded). A notification alone never
   authorizes work.
4. **Hold until the process truly finishes** — including background
   execution. If the shell returned but the job still runs, you still hold
   the permit (that is the point).
5. **Release promptly** — success or failure. Release is idempotent; calling
   it twice is safe, calling it after a crash-recovery release is safe.
6. **Cancel** queued requests you no longer need, so someone else can have
   the capacity.

Notes on the details:

- `op_key` makes duplicate acquires idempotent: if your pending request for
  the same op already exists, `acquire` returns it instead of a second one.
  Use a stable key per distinct operation (e.g. `build/auth-module`), and
  different keys for different operations.
- Offers have a **claim window** (default 30s). If it lapses, the request
  becomes **paused** — capacity moves on and your request waits until you
  explicitly `rejoin(request_id)`. If you know you can't start in time,
  `decline` instead of letting it expire.

### Sleeping until your turn (`wait_for_turn`)

Rule 2 says keep doing light work while queued — but sometimes there is
nothing useful left. `wait_for_turn(request_id?, timeout_ms?)` is the honest
way to idle: a **bounded blocking sleep** over one of your queued, offered
or paused requests (default: your most urgent one). When capacity reaches
you mid-sleep, the offer is **auto-claimed inside the claim window** and
you wake holding the permit (`granted`, `permit_token` + `auto_claimed:
true` in the response).

Every resolution is a structured result, never an opaque error:

- `granted` — your turn came; the permit is already claimed for you.
- `still_queued` — the bound expired; you get your queue position, queue
  length and who is holding the capacity. Call it again to keep sleeping.
- `paused` — your offer expired or was declined meanwhile; `next_action`
  has the rejoin instructions.
- `cancelled` — the request was cancelled/declined/reclaimed meanwhile.
- `not_found` — the request ended, or the daemon restarted (queues are
  ephemeral); acquire again.

The sleep is bounded and **safe by construction**: it holds no permit and
no capacity, cancelling the tool call just stops the local sleep (nothing
is orphaned — your request keeps its queue position), and a daemon restart
mid-sleep resolves promptly with `not_found` instead of hanging. `timeout_ms`
defaults to 600000 (10 minutes) and is clamped to the machine's
`maxTurnWaitMs` cap (`get_config` shows it; `configure` can set it, valid
range 1000–3600000 ms). `timeout_ms: 0` means check-only. The CLI form is
`load-lock wait --id <request-id> --timeout <ms>`.

### Sleeping through execution (`wait_for_completion`)

The queue phase has `wait_for_turn`; the execution phase has its counterpart.
After you start a heavy job, do not guess sleeps or poll `job_status` in a
loop — sleep honestly: one bounded call that **wakes promptly when the job
finishes**. There are two mechanisms, and the identifier picks the right one:

- **`job_id` of a `run_with_permit` job** (the job belongs to your adapter
  process): the wake is the child's exact `exit` event — no polling, prompt,
  with the exact exit code and an output tail. The same thing in one call:
  `run_with_permit(..., wait: true)` starts the job and sleeps through it.
- **`request_id` of a daemon-tracked permit** (`attach_pid` etc. — the daemon
  is not the parent): the daemon holds the wait server-side and wakes it when
  its liveness sweep observes the process gone (worst case one sweep interval,
  default 5s). The permit is **released before you are woken**, so a woken
  agent sees the capacity freed. The CLI form is
  `load-lock wait --job <request-id> --timeout <ms>`.

Every resolution is a structured result, never an opaque error:

- `finished` — exit code, output tail, duration, and the permit-release
  state (`permit_released`; if the release round-trip was still in flight
  the `detail` says so — verify with `status` if in doubt).
- `still_running` — the bound expired mid-execution; this is a **checkpoint**,
  not a failure. Call again; a long job is a handful of long sleeps, not a
  poll loop.
- `timeout` — this wait call was aborted/cancelled (harness tool timeout,
  AbortSignal). The job is untouched; call again.
- `job_unknown` — no such job/request, or the permit was reclaimed/expired
  meanwhile (e.g. the daemon or adapter restarted); re-check before
  proceeding.
- `stopped_by_request` — the job or permit was stopped by an explicit
  (admin) action; re-acquire before running more heavy work.

The sleep is bounded and safe by construction: it holds no permit and no
capacity itself, and for daemon-tracked waits `timeout_ms` is clamped to the
machine's `maxTurnWaitMs` cap (same as `wait_for_turn`; adapter-parented
waits default to 600000). `timeout_ms: 0` means check-only. A daemon restart
mid-wait is handled transparently (tracked permits survive restarts via the
journal); against an older daemon the client falls back to a light
events-based poll with the same structured results. Cancelling the call
never kills the job. If someone calls `job_stop` while you are waiting, you
wake with `stopped_by_request`.

## 3. Running heavy work (lifecycle options)

How you start the work determines how reliably the permit cleans up after
you — pick the best available:

1. **`run_with_permit(permit_token, command)`** — the helper spawns your
   command in its own process group, atomically associates it with the
   permit, and auto-releases when the process group *actually finishes*
   (including background children). Sleep through the execution with
   `wait_for_completion(job_id)` (or pass `wait: true` to fire-and-wait in
   one call); quick-check with `job_status(job_id)`; kill with
   `job_stop(job_id)`. Do **not** manually release a permit you handed to
   `run_with_permit`.
2. **`attach_pid(permit_token, pid)`** — you spawned the process yourself;
   the daemon now tracks that pid (and its process group) and releases when
   it is confirmed dead. Works for `... &` background jobs whose parent
   shell exits.
3. **`mark_started(permit_token)`** — no observable process (e.g. you call
   an external service). The permit is held under a lease (default 15 min)
   that is kept alive by heartbeats from your harness integration. Honest
   limitation: if your agent process dies silently, the lease eventually
   frees the capacity, but during that window nobody can guarantee the
   unseen work has stopped. Prefer 1 or 2 whenever possible.

If you `acquire` and get **granted** but then fail to start the work within
the start deadline (default 120s), the permit is automatically reclaimed —
nobody is stranded by a crashed claimant, and neither are you.

The equivalent CLI forms exist for shell-driven flows:

```sh
load-lock acquire --reason "cargo test" --op-key "test/core"      # prints JSON
load-lock run --permit <permit-token> -- cargo test --quiet       # tracks + releases
# or acquire+run in one go:
load-lock run --reason "nightly build" -- npm run build
load-lock wait --id <request-id> --timeout 120000                # sleep until your turn → auto-claim
load-lock help                                                    # one-screen usage of every command
```

## 4. Reading state

- `status(pool?)` — snapshot of the whole machine: holders (with phase,
  reason, age), outstanding offers, queue depth, paused requests.
- `pending()` — *your* requests and offers (with claim tokens).
- `inspect_machine()` — cores/memory incl. cgroup limits, pressure.
- `get_config()` / `configure(expected_version, changes, reason)` —
  versioned CAS budget changes; every change is recorded with author and
  rationale. On `version_conflict`, re-read and retry with the fresh
  version.
- Events have durable ids; after reconnects or restarts, consult
  `events(since)` rather than assuming.

## 5. Cleanup and failure etiquette

| Situation | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Work finished (success or failure) | `release` |
| Queued request no longer needed | `cancel` |
| Claim window will lapse before you can start | `decline` the offer |
| Offer already expired (`offer_expired`) | `rejoin` when actually ready |
| Your harness session is about to end with a live tracked job | Nothing — `run_with_permit`/`attach_pid` jobs release themselves when done |
| You suspect a stuck holder | `status` → `recover list` diagnostics, and discuss with the operator before `force-release` |

Never force-release someone else's permit without checking `recover list`
first — a long hold with a live tracked process is working as intended.

## 6. Suggested internal parallelism

When you hold the permit, you own a share of the machine — bound your own
work too: prefer e.g. `cargo test -j 2` or a bounded test-worker count over
unbounded parallelism, and publish what you did via
`configure(... guidance ...)` notes if it should become convention.

## 7. Keeping load-lock itself current

If load-lock tells you its adapter copy is newer than the installed CLI
(`load-lock: this load-lock adapter copy (vX) is newer than the installed
CLI (vY). Run \`load-lock update\` ...`), run it **as an ordinary command**
(CLI: `load-lock update`; MCP/plugin: spawn the CLI or tell the user) —
never try to install anything behind the notice; it is notify-only.
`load-lock update --check` is the safe dry run: exit 0 = up to date,
1 = update available (or this copy cannot self-apply it — repo checkouts
and opencode-managed copies are refused honestly), 70 = failure. A
successful apply restarts the service itself; you do not need to.

# load-lock architecture

load-lock is a cross-harness coordination plugin for parallel coding agents. It
provides a machine-wide counting semaphore: before doing resource-intensive
work (builds, test suites, long compiles), an agent acquires a permit; while
queued it keeps doing light work; when capacity frees up it receives a FIFO
offer, claims it, runs the heavy work, and releases. Coordination is
cooperative and advisory — nothing wraps or rewrites shell commands, and agents
decide for themselves what counts as "heavy".

## Why a small dedicated service (vs extending something existing)

We evaluated the existing landscape before building:

- **WorkOS Airlock** (the closest name match) is a commercial, cloud-hosted
  *authorization* gateway for agents: it approves or denies tool calls
  (agent identity, intent, egress policies) via WorkOS Pipes. It answers "is
  this agent allowed to do this?", not "does this machine have spare capacity
  right now?". It has no machine-local state, no queue, no offers, and no
  process-lifecycle tracking. Smaller GitHub projects named "airlock"
  (an agent type-checker gate, an MCP egress allow-list) are similarly
  unrelated.
- **mic-lock** (npm) provides local sticky locks for shared test resources,
  but it is a single lock with no counting semaphore, no FIFO queue, no
  offer/claim protocol, no harness integration, and no automatic cleanup.
- **flock-wrapper scripts** (advisory lock around a command) cannot work
  across harness tool calls: the acquire step is a short-lived process that
  must exit before the agent does its real work, releasing the lock with it.
  A `flock` held by a process that has already exited protects nothing. (We
  do use an flock-style spawn lock internally — for daemon bootstrapping —
  but never for permits.)

No existing project combines a counting semaphore, FIFO offers with claim
tokens, per-agent identity, automatic permit cleanup tied to real process
lifetimes, and harness instruction/notification adapters. The coordination
state is small and its lifetime is the machine, not a repo — so a small
dedicated daemon plus thin per-harness adapters is the right shape. Extending
a larger system (e.g. a build tool) would couple the budget to one harness
and inherit unrelated constraints.

## Core design

**One daemon, one budget.** A single `load-lock` daemon process per machine
owns all state. Every client — any harness, any repo, any worktree — talks to
the same Unix-domain socket (named pipe `\\.\pipe\load-lock` on Windows),
so all sessions share one capacity budget
regardless of working directory. The default configuration is one pool
`heavy` with capacity 1; pools, capacity, and timings are changed at runtime
through `configure` (versioned compare-and-swap, persisted with author +
reason). The state directory lives outside any checkout
(`$XDG_STATE_HOME/load-lock`, default `~/.local/state/load-lock`, overridable
via `LOAD_LOCK_STATE_DIR`).

**Single-threaded atomicity.** The daemon is one Node process; every state
mutation happens on one event loop turn. There is no interleaving between
"check capacity" and "grant" — acquisition is atomic by construction, and
there is no window in which a release can be missed between a failed check
and queue registration. `acquire` either grants or registers in the queue in
one operation; there is no separate failed-acquire/subscribe sequence that
could miss a wakeup.

**FIFO offers with claim tokens.** When capacity frees, the daemon reserves
it and creates an offer for the head of the queue: an opaque claim token with
an expiry (default 30s). The offer is delivered to the agent (see
notifications below); heavy work starts only after a successful `claim`,
which atomically converts the offer into a permit. Outstanding offers consume
capacity, so an unclaimed offer cannot admit a second agent over budget. If
the offer expires, capacity passes to the next waiter and the expired request
becomes **paused** — it will not be re-offered until the agent explicitly
`rejoin`s. This prevents endless recycling of offers to absent agents.

**Permit lifecycle (automatic cleanup).** A permit moves through phases:

1. **Claimed, awaiting execution** — has a configurable start deadline
   (default 120s). If execution never starts, the permit is reclaimed.
2. **Running, tracked** — associated with a real OS process via
   `attach_pid`/`run_with_permit` (pid + process-group id + `/proc` start
   time). The permit lives as long as the associated job: parent shells may
   exit, background children keep the group alive, and the daemon
   auto-releases only on confirmed termination. It is never auto-expired
   merely because time passed. PID reuse is defended by comparing
   `/proc/<pid>/stat` start times.
3. **Running, untracked** — `mark_started` for jobs the daemon cannot
   observe. Held under a lease (default 15 min) kept alive by heartbeats
   (the MCP server and OpenCode plugin heartbeat automatically every 30s).
   This is an explicit tradeoff: a lease cannot simultaneously guarantee
   prompt reclamation and never overlap an unobserved surviving process.
   We reclaim when the owner stops heartbeating, and we document the
   residual risk instead of claiming a guarantee we can't make.

Explicit `release` always remains available and is idempotent (a duplicate or
late release is a no-op, not an error). `admin release` / `recover
force-release` exists for humans with holder/job diagnostics.

**Association is atomic.** `run_with_permit` spawns the job (its own process
group) and only then associates pid+pgid with the permit in a single daemon
operation; a reclamation racing the start loses cleanly (stale token /
wrong-state error), and a failed start kills the process group immediately.
Background execution is handled honestly: the helper returns after *the whole
process group* finishes, never merely when a shell returns a task id.

**Identity.** Per-agent identity is derived from the harness session
(issues #49/#50): an explicit `agent_id` / `--agent` / `LOAD_LOCK_AGENT`
wins, else a harness session id (OpenCode `sessionID`, Claude Code
`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, hook `session_id`), else the stable harness
ancestor process on Linux, so every wiring of one session (CLI, MCP
server, hooks) acts as one agent (details in
[COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md#session-identity-per-harness)); every entry also records an agent label,
cwd, op key (for idempotent duplicate suppression), and reason. Idempotency:
a duplicate `acquire` from the same agent for the same pending op key returns
the existing request rather than a second one; multiple distinct ops per
agent are supported. All tokens (permits, offers) are opaque; releasing or
claiming with someone else's token fails.

**Restart behavior.** Config is persisted (atomic write + rename). Held
permits are journaled: on daemon restart, tracked permits are reconciled
against real process liveness (dead ⇒ released, alive ⇒ kept, same tokens
still valid), claimed permits keep their original start deadline, untracked
permits get a fresh lease window, and a release arriving late for an entry
that was reconciled is idempotent. Queued *and offered* requests are journaled
too (issue #34): they are re-queued FIFO by original enqueue time with the
same request ids (idempotent re-acquire keeps working), entries offered at
crash time restart as queued and are re-offered with fresh tokens — so a
restart no longer silently drops a queue position. The daemon auto-spawns on
the next client connection, and a *self-ordered* restart (version handshake:
a newer client than the daemon) persists state and respawns onto the newer
client's copy (#53; same argv when that copy can't be validated) — see the update lifecycle in
[OPERATIONS.md](OPERATIONS.md#update-lifecycle).

**Persisted format compatibility (issue #51).** Several runtime copies may
share one state dir, so a downgrade is possible: a newer daemon dies and an
older client starts its older copy, which must then load files the newer one
wrote. `config.json` carries a top-level `formatVersion` (absent = 0, the
pre-versioning format); the journal stays a bare JSON array (what every
released daemon reads) with `formatVersion` stamped on each entry. The
promise, in both directions:

- Format changes are **additive**. A reader never rejects a file because its
  `formatVersion` is higher than its own; it uses what it understands.
- Unknown fields are **never dropped destructively**: top-level and
  `config`/pool/guidance fields of `config.json` survive a rewrite (e.g. a
  `configure`), and unknown fields on a journal entry are written back while
  that entry lives. Each writer stamps its *own* `formatVersion`, so readers
  must treat fields from a newer format as possibly stale.
- Unknown journal entry kinds (a `state` this version doesn't know) and
  malformed entries are **skipped**, never fatal; the count is reported in the
  `daemon_recovered` event. A held entry with an unknown `phase` is kept as an
  untracked permit with a fresh lease (capacity stays accounted; the lease
  reclaims it if nobody heartbeats).
- An incompatible change would use a **new file name**, never reinterpret
  `config.json` / `journal.json`.

## Three layers: daemon, runtime copies, harness wiring

load-lock reaches a machine through many entry points (a skill, an MCP
registration, a harness plugin, ACE, `npm i -g` + `load-lock install`), and
users mix them across harnesses and over time. The design rule (issue #47):
**any combination, installed in any order, gives one working budget.** It
holds because load-lock is split into three layers with different
multiplicity:

| Layer | Per machine | What it is | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Daemon** | exactly 1 (one socket, one state dir) | the long-lived process that owns all state, started on demand by whichever client connects first (`src/shared/client.ts`) | the newest copy runs it |
| **Runtime copies** | many | installed copies of the npm package: global npm/bun, the npx cache, OpenCode's plugin cache, a git checkout; the Claude Code plugin's launcher picks one of them | copies interoperate in both directions; none "owns" the daemon |
| **Harness wiring** | ideally 1 per harness, possibly several | MCP registrations, hooks, policy text, skill copies, written by a plugin, ACE, `load-lock install` or by hand | duplicates are **harmless**, not merely discouraged |

**Duplicates are harmless.** Each overlap is defused where the singleton
lives, not by hoping the user cleans up:

- *Hooks*: two wirings of the same hook (loose + plugin, two plugins, ACE)
  both fire, but the daemon's `hook_once` lets only the first act — one
  policy injection, one Stop continuation, one idle watcher per session
  (see "Duplicate hook wiring is harmless" below).
- *MCP servers*: two registrations in one session (e.g. ACE's `mcp.json` +
  the plugin's bundled server) are two processes with the **same**
  session-derived identity (see Identity above), so an `acquire` through
  one shows up in `pending` through the other. Both talk to the one daemon.
- *Skill copies*: identical text; the skill only tells the agent how to
  reach the daemon.

Housekeeping is still offered: `load-lock setup` lists every integration
per harness and, with `--yes`, converges each harness to one wiring at its
highest rung (see [OPERATIONS.md](OPERATIONS.md#load-lock-setup-what-is-installed-where)).
Correctness never depends on running it.

**Compatibility promise between copies.** Because several copies of
different versions talk to one daemon and one state dir:

- every client envelope carries its version and package root; a strictly
  newer client makes the daemon persist state and respawn onto that
  client's copy (#52/#53, see "Runtime copies and the restart hint"
  below), with one attempt per version;
- the persisted files are versioned and additive in both directions, so
  an older daemon started after a newer one died reads the newer files
  safely (#51, "Persisted format compatibility" above);
- newer client features degrade against an older daemon instead of
  failing: hooks without `hook_once` act as before, `wait_for_completion`
  falls back to an events-based poll.

The **install ladder** built on top of this (skill → MCP server → harness
plugin, plus `npm i -g` + `load-lock install`) is described in
[OPERATIONS.md](OPERATIONS.md#the-install-ladder); which rung each harness
reaches is in [COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md#rung-per-harness).

## Notification honesty

A critical constraint discovered by research: **no harness reliably pushes
MCP-server-initiated notifications into model context.** MCP transports
having a notification mechanism says nothing about whether the harness wakes
an idle agent or injects into context. load-lock therefore uses four
mechanisms, and labels exactly which apply per harness:

1. **Tool-boundary delivery (always available).** Every load-lock tool
   result and every `status`/`pending` call carries the caller's current
   offers (with claim tokens) — an agent performing light work discovers its
   offer at its next tool call, without polling.
2. **Bounded blocking wait.** `acquire(wait_ms)` blocks briefly (default
   5s) inside the tool call and auto-claims if capacity frees during the
   wait. For longer sleeps there is one shared client-side
   implementation, `waitForTurn` (`src/shared/wait-turn.ts`), surfaced as
   the CLI `wait` command, the MCP `wait_for_turn` tool and the OpenCode
   plugin's `load_lock_wait_for_turn` tool: it polls light
   events+pending pulls on the local socket, auto-claims inside the
   offer window, returns structured results on every path (granted /
   still_queued with position / paused / cancelled / not_found), is
   bounded by `timeout_ms` (capped by the `maxTurnWaitMs` config), and —
   being purely client-side — holds no permit, consumes no capacity, and
   can never orphan a daemon-side waiter when the harness cancels the
   tool mid-sleep. Daemon restarts are detected via the event cursor and
   resolve bounded. No model-authored busy-polling required.
   The execution phase has its mirror, `wait_for_completion`
   (`src/shared/wait-completion.ts`), surfaced as the same CLI `wait`
   command (`--job`), the MCP/OpenCode `wait_for_completion` tool and
   `run_with_permit(wait: true)`. Two wake mechanisms: for
   adapter-parented jobs (`run_with_permit`) the adapter awaits the
   child's `exit` event directly — exact exit code, no polling; for
   daemon-tracked permits (`attach_pid`) the daemon holds the wait
   server-side and wakes it when the liveness sweep observes the pid
   gone — mirroring `wait_for_turn`'s bounded-sleep shape (checkpoint
   results on every path: finished / still_running / timeout /
   job_unknown / stopped_by_request). Ordering guarantee: the permit is
   released (capacity freed) *before* waiters are woken. Restarts are
   transparent for tracked permits (journal restore), and against older
   daemons the client degrades to a light events-based poll with the
   same structured results.
3. **Idle wakeup where the harness genuinely supports it.**
   - OpenCode (live-verified): the native plugin watches daemon events and
     calls `ctx.session.synthetic(...)`, delivering the offer (with token)
     to an idle session at its next execution boundary — it never
     interrupts an in-flight shell command.
   - Claude Code (live-verified in Docker with the loose install; the
     plugin's hooks are not yet live-verified, #63): a `Stop` hook checks for cwd-matching
     offers and continues the session with a claim instruction; an async
     `await-offer` watcher with `asyncRewake: true` wakes idle sessions.
   - Codex CLI (live-verified in Docker): `Stop` hook with `decision: "block"`
     continuation. Note: Codex async background hooks do **not** start a new
     turn — documented as a limitation.
4. **Durable event identities.** All events have monotonic IDs; agents can
   pull owner-filtered events since a cursor and deduplicate after reconnect
   or daemon restart. A notification NEVER grants permission — only
   `claim(offer_token)` does; expired offers are rejected and stale
   notifications authorize nothing.

## Instruction delivery (policy teaching)

The behavioral policy (acquire before heavy work, keep doing light work
while queued, claim before starting, hold until the process truly finishes,
release promptly, cancel unneeded work, use inspect/configure when the
budget needs adjustment) is delivered per harness using its real mechanism,
and restored after context compaction:

- **OpenCode**: plugin `context` hook injects the brief on every model call
  (compaction-proof, live-verified), plus a registered skill with the full
  guide.
- **Claude Code**: `SessionStart` hook (re-fires after `compact`), from
  either the `load-lock-plugin` plugin or the loose install; the loose
  install adds a `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` section + skill, the plugin ships
  neither (full guide via the `agent_guide` MCP tool).
- **Codex CLI**: `SessionStart` hook (matcher `compact`) + `SubagentStart`
  hook + `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` section (hooks require the interactive
  hook-trust review once; live-verified in Docker).
- Other harnesses: MCP server `instructions` + a global instructions file
  snippet where the harness supports one (see COMPATIBILITY.md).

Policy is short (one brief, no repeated reminders), reinforced by tool
names/descriptions, and never interrupts ordinary work with approval
prompts.

**Duplicate hook wiring is harmless (issue #54).** Loose hooks, a plugin
and ACE wiring may all be installed at once, so one harness event can fire
the same load-lock hook several times. The daemon is the singleton, so it
drops duplicates: each hook handler first calls `hook_once` with the key
`(harness, session_id, event, occurrence)`; only the first caller acts, the
rest exit 0 silently. The occurrence separates legitimate repeats:
SessionStart uses its `source` (a later `compact` re-injects the policy),
Stop hooks (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) use the offer token being delivered
(each offer becomes at most one continuation per session). Keys expire on
their own (default 60s) and are never persisted; the `await-offer` watcher
instead *holds* its key for its connection's lifetime, so a session has at
most one live watcher and the key frees when the watcher exits. Hooks fail
open: no session id, a daemon without `hook_once` (`unknown method`), or
any error means the hook acts exactly as before.

## Failure modes covered

| Failure | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Agent disconnects mid-heavy-work | Permit retained; tracked job keeps capacity until the real process finishes; untracked job's lease survives until heartbeats stop |
| Agent process crashes | Tracked permit auto-releases on confirmed process death; untracked reclaims after lease expiry |
| Background job outlives the tool call | pgid tracking retains the permit until the whole group exits |
| Daemon crash/restart | Auto-respawn on next connect; journal reconciliation of held permits (conservative: dead ⇒ released, alive ⇒ kept); queued/offered requests re-queued FIFO with same ids, offered entries re-offered with fresh tokens |
| Stale/forged token | Opaque tokens; wrong-owner claim/release rejected; expired offers rejected with a precise error |
| Forgotten release | start deadline (claimed), process death (tracked), lease expiry (untracked), plus human `recover force-release` |
| PID reuse | `/proc` start-time comparison |
| Config change while offers outstanding | Capacity increase admits queued agents immediately; capacity decrease lets holders finish and delays new admissions; outstanding offers keep their reservations |
| Duplicate claims/releases | Idempotent or precise `stale_token`/`offer_expired` errors, never double effects |

### Runtime copies and the restart hint

`daemon.json` records the daemon's package root and version, and
`runtimes.json` the copies seen via the handshake (#52). When a strictly
newer client connects, the daemon respawns onto that client's copy (#53)
if the envelope's `clientRoot` names a `@aron98/load-lock` package whose
on-disk version equals the claimed `clientVersion` and which ships
`dist/core/daemon-main.js`; otherwise it reruns its own argv. The
`LOAD_LOCK_RESTARTED_FOR` marker keeps one restart per version either way.

Security: the hint arrives over the daemon's socket, which only the same
user can reach. Following it grants no privilege the client did not
already have — that client could run the same file itself. The checks
exist to avoid respawning onto garbage (wrong package, mismatched version,
missing entry), not as a trust boundary.

## Extension points

The protocol already carries weights (a request may ask for >1 units of
capacity; admission is FIFO with head-of-line blocking) and multiple pools;
the machine currently uses one pool by default but accepts arbitrary pool
names through the same code paths. Adding a second budget (e.g. `network`)
is configuration, not code.

The read-only status surface also extends without protocol changes: the
`status` + `events` (durable ids) + `watch` + `inspect` methods are enough
to build live viewers. `load-lock dashboard` (alias `top`) and the OpenCode TUI panel
(`src/dashboard/`) are exactly that — pure view-model shaping over the
library client (`./shared/client`), never CLI-output scraping, and never
acquiring a permit themselves. Any future harness UI can reuse the same
`src/dashboard/` pipeline.

#### Multiple copies of load-lock (opencode)

`install --harness opencode` registers the **bare package name** in
`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, so opencode maintains its own private
copy of load-lock under
`~/.cache/opencode/npm/@aron98/load-lock@latest/<timestamp>/node_modules/@aron98/load-lock/`,
refreshed on opencode's schedule. That copy is *separate* from a globally
installed CLI on PATH, and the two can drift (this was observed on a real
machine with cache copies at 0.1.2, 1.0.0, 1.1.0 and 1.2.1 — issue #34).

Which copy is authoritative for what:

- **opencode plugin behavior** — the cache copy. Updated by opencode itself
  (it refreshes the cache entry); you cannot reliably update it by hand.
- **CLI commands** (`load-lock status`, `service`, `doctor`, …) — the copy on
  PATH (typically a global install via npm/bun). Update it with your usual
  global install command, or `load-lock update` (since #38), which detects
  the package manager from the copy's location and refuses to touch copies
  it does not manage: it will not "update" the opencode cache copy (opencode
  owns it) nor a git checkout (your git workflow owns it), and it restarts
  the service after a successful apply.
- **The daemon's code** — whichever copy spawned it (usually the CLI copy,
  since auto-spawn and `service start` run from the CLI client code). The
  version handshake makes a daemon self-restart onto updated code when a
  newer client contacts it. Since #53 the respawn moves onto the newer
  client's own copy (validated from its `clientRoot` hint), so a daemon
  spawned from a different copy than the one you updated follows the
  newer client. Clients older than #52 send no `clientRoot`; for them the
  respawn reuses the daemon's original argv and only picks up an in-place
  update of its spawning copy — `load-lock service restart` (since #38)
  re-spawns it from the current CLI copy.
- **npx-launched copies** (since #57) — skill / ACE / pinned MCP entries run
  `npx -y @aron98/load-lock@<pin>`, which installs a copy under the npm
  cache at `~/.npm/_npx/<hash>/node_modules/@aron98/load-lock/` (or under
  `$npm_config_cache/_npx`; `%LocalAppData%\npm-cache\_npx` on Windows).
  `doctor` lists these as `npx-cache`. They are owned by the pin that
  launches them: `load-lock update` refuses to touch them and points at
  bumping the pinned version (or the ACE artifact) instead.

The mirror drift — a *newer* adapter copy (opencode refreshed its cache)
with an *older* CLI on PATH — surfaces at adapter init (issue #38): the
plugin/MCP server prints one clear notice naming `load-lock update` and
embeds it in the injected context/instructions. Notify only, never
auto-install. See
[OPERATIONS.md](OPERATIONS.md#adapter-init-drift-notice) for the
in-memory-staleness limitation (a running session keeps the old adapter
code until the harness restarts).

`load-lock doctor` lists every copy it can find (PATH-resolved CLI, this
running copy, opencode cache copies) with versions and warns when they
drift. Detection is best-effort (never crashes on missing paths) and was
contract-tested with planted copies; the drift scenario itself was
observed live on this machine before the feature existed.

## Session identity per harness

The daemon routes offers, `pending` and op-key duplicate suppression by agent
id, so each harness session needs exactly one id, whichever wiring (CLI, MCP
server, hook) made the call. The default identity of the CLI (issue #49) and
of the MCP server (issue #50) comes from the shared resolver in
`src/shared/identity.ts`, first match wins:

1. explicit override: `--agent` (CLI), `agent_id` (MCP tools), or
   `LOAD_LOCK_AGENT`;
2. a harness session env var exported to the processes the harness spawns:
   `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` → `claude-code:<session_id>` (the same value hooks
   receive as `session_id`; verified on Claude Code 2.1.x), and
   `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID` → the bare `sessionID` (exported by OpenCode's bash
   tool; verified on opencode 2.1.1). The bare id is exactly the native
   plugin's agent id, so CLI calls from an OpenCode shell share the plugin's
   identity;
3. the stable harness ancestor process (Linux): walk up from the CLI's parent
   past shells and launcher wrappers (`sh`/`bash`/`zsh`/…, `env`, `timeout`,
   `npm`/`npx`, nested `load-lock`) to the first other ancestor, identified as
   `proc:<pid>:<start time>` (pid-reuse safe via `/proc/<pid>/stat`), labelled
   `<comm>:<pid>`. This covers harnesses without a verified env var (Codex,
   Cursor, Gemini CLI, …), since one session = one long-lived harness process;
4. otherwise (no harness ancestor, or no `/proc` — macOS/Windows without a
   session env var) the legacy default: `cli:$USER@$HOSTNAME` for the CLI, a
   random per-process `agt_…` id for the MCP server.

So two MCP registrations in one session (plugin-bundled + standalone) share
one id: an `acquire` through one shows in `pending` through the other, and
both heartbeat the same id (idempotent). The CLI and the MCP server of one
session share an id too when both see the same session env var or the same
harness ancestor; whether a harness exports its session env var to MCP
server processes is not verified for every harness.

Labels stay human-readable: session-derived ids get a short holder label
(`claude-code:ee690007`, `codex:12345`); explicit ids label themselves.

# Operating load-lock

## Install

Requirements: Node 20+, Linux (macOS works with the limitations noted below;
Windows has a named-pipe transport adapter — implemented and unit-tested on
Linux via platform injection, not yet verified on a Windows machine; see the
Windows section at the bottom).

### The install ladder

load-lock can be installed at several levels ("rungs"). Each rung works on
its own, and a higher rung only adds capability. Installing more than one,
in any order, is safe: there is still one daemon and one budget, one
identity per session, and duplicate hooks are dropped by the daemon (see
[ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md#three-layers-daemon-runtime-copies-harness-wiring)).

| Rung | What you install | Runtime it runs | What the agent gets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | **Skill only** (`skills/load-lock/SKILL.md`) | the load-lock MCP tools if listed, else `load-lock` on PATH, else `npx -y @aron98/load-lock@<version>` (pinned in the skill) | the full permit lifecycle through the CLI (`run`, `wait`, `acquire` / `claim` / `release`, `cancel`); the first call starts the daemon. No idle wakeup, no policy injection, nothing after compaction |
| 1 | **MCP server** (`npx -y @aron98/load-lock@<version> mcp`) | the pinned npx copy | the tools; your offers in every load-lock tool result; `wait_for_turn` / `wait_for_completion` bounded sleeps; the policy in the MCP `instructions` where the harness shows them; the `agent_guide` tool |
| 2 | **Harness plugin**: Claude Code `load-lock-plugin`, OpenCode npm plugin `@aron98/load-lock` | Claude Code: the plugin launcher (PATH CLI if new enough, else a known copy, else pinned npx); OpenCode: its own plugin cache copy | everything the harness supports: tools, policy at session start that survives compaction, offer wakeups at turn ends and while idle |
| — | **`npm i -g` + `load-lock install --harness <h>`** | the global CLI | the same wiring as loose config files. The only route for harnesses without a plugin, and the escape hatch where plugins aren't allowed |

Each rung points at the next one once: the skill, the MCP `instructions`
and the session-start brief end with a one-line pointer to
[`load-lock setup`](#load-lock-setup-what-is-installed-where), which lists
what is installed where and converges it. The rung each harness can reach
is in [COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md#rung-per-harness).

How to install each rung:

- **Skill (0).** Through ACE (the `load-lock` skill artifact, see
  [Installing via ACE](#installing-via-ace)), or copy `skills/load-lock/`
  (shipped in the npm package and the repo) into your harness's skills
  directory. `load-lock install --harness claude-code` also copies it to
  `~/.claude/skills/load-lock/`.
- **MCP server (1).** Through ACE (the `ace/mcp` artifact), or register a
  stdio server named `load-lock` with command `npx` and args
  `["-y", "@aron98/load-lock@<version>", "mcp"]`, exactly what
  `ace/mcp/mcp.json` declares. `load-lock mcp` is the same server as the
  `load-lock-mcp` binary. With a global install,
  `load-lock install --harness generic` prints a snippet that runs that
  copy instead of npx.
- **Plugin (2).** Claude Code: see [Claude Code plugin](#claude-code-plugin).
  OpenCode: add `@aron98/load-lock` to the `plugins` array of
  `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (OpenCode downloads and updates it),
  or let `load-lock install --harness opencode` register it.
- **Loose wiring.** The installers below.

never matched its own entries — duplicate installs and hooks that survived

### `load-lock setup`: what is installed where

`load-lock setup [--project <dir>] [--json]` lists every load-lock
integration it finds, for every harness `install` supports (the project
defaults to the cwd). It is **read-only**: it never writes a file.

For each harness it reports:

- **what** it found: plugins (Claude Code `enabledPlugins` entries named
  `load-lock-plugin@…`, OpenCode `plugin` / `plugins` entries), MCP
  registrations (user and project scope, including ACE's `.mcp.json`
  `servers` patch), loose hooks, policy sections / rule files, skill
  copies, and omac sandbox grants;
- **who** wrote each entry: `installer` (the exact shape `load-lock
  install` writes), `harness` (the harness's own plugin state), `ace`
  (an `.ace.json` stamp sits next to it), or `other` (manual, npx, …);
- **which copy** an entry runs, and whether that copy is gone (stale);
- the **rung**: `plugin`, `loose` (`load-lock install` wiring), `MCP only`,
  `skill only`, or `not installed`;
- **findings**: loose hooks next to an active plugin, the MCP server
  registered more than once (a Claude Code plugin's bundled server counts),
  hooks from more than one copy, duplicate hook entries, several skill
  copies, stale entries, disabled plugins.

It ends with the runtime copies: those on disk (as in `doctor`), the copy
the daemon runs (`daemon.json`), and the copies the daemon has seen.

An ACE-installed Claude plugin (unzipped into `.claude/skills/<name>/`) is
listed but not counted as an active plugin: whether Claude Code loads it
there is not verified yet (#63).

#### Converging: `load-lock setup --yes`

After the inventory, `setup` prints a **plan** that brings every harness
that already has some load-lock wiring to the recommended layout: the
highest rung available, exactly one of each. Without `--yes` it is a dry
run. `--yes` applies it (`--json` adds `plan` and `applied`). Harnesses with
nothing installed are left alone; the plan names them once.

The plan only uses moves the installers can reverse:

| Situation | Step |
|---|---|
| Claude Code plugin enabled **and** loose `install` wiring | `remove-loose`: drop the loose MCP server, hooks and `CLAUDE.md` section (the plugin provides them). The skill stays: the plugin ships none. Undo: `load-lock install --harness claude-code --legacy`. |
| Installer wiring incomplete, pointing at a missing copy, or hooks from several copies / duplicated | `install`: remove the installer-shaped hooks of every copy (and a stale codex `[mcp_servers.load-lock]` block), then `load-lock install --harness <h>` from the running copy |
| Only an MCP registration or only the skill | `install` (moves up to the installer's rung) |
| Anything not written by `load-lock install` (plugin state, ACE entries, manual / npx entries, extra skill copies) | `manual`: printed with what to remove or run (`/plugin uninstall …`), never applied |

Guards, each turning an `install` into a `manual` step:

- a foreign entry sits in the slot `install` would overwrite (e.g. a
  hand-written `mcpServers.load-lock`);
- the Claude Code skill directory is managed by ACE (`.ace.json`);
- the running copy lives in the npx or opencode cache, which npm may prune
  (install globally first);
- `cursor` / `roo-code` write into the project, so they are only refreshed
  when the project already has their installer wiring.

`load-lock uninstall --harness <h>` still removes everything load-lock
added, after a converge as before it. The MCP instructions and the
session-start brief end with a one-line pointer to `load-lock setup`.

### Claude Code plugin

Instead of `install --harness claude-code`, Claude Code can load load-lock
as a plugin (issue #61). The repo root is a marketplace
(`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`) listing one plugin, `load-lock-plugin`,
in `plugins/claude-code/`:

```text
/plugin marketplace add aron98/load-lock
/plugin install load-lock-plugin@load-lock
```

- **MCP server** `load-lock`, declared inline in `plugin.json` and started
  through the launcher (`--bin load-lock-mcp`). Tools are named
  `mcp__plugin_load-lock-plugin_load-lock__<tool>`.
- **Hooks** in `hooks/hooks.json`, the same three as the loose install:
  `SessionStart` (policy + machine summary), `Stop` (offer continuation)
  and the `async` + `asyncRewake` `await-offer` watcher. Each runs in shell
  form, one command string `node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/load-lock.mjs"
  hook claude-code <event>` with the root quoted (#63). Shell form is the
  long-documented hook shape; exec form (`command` + `args`) has no
  documented minimum Claude Code version. The string has no shell
  metacharacters, so ACE's `plugin_hooks_command_safe` check passes.
- **No skill and no CLAUDE.md section.** The policy arrives through the
  SessionStart hook (re-fired after compaction), and the full guide through
  the `agent_guide` MCP tool. Install the `load-lock` skill separately if
  wanted. The plugin is not named `load-lock`, so it doesn't clash with the
  skill on ACE (#64).
- **Runtime**: the plugin ships no `dist/`. See [Plugin launcher](#plugin-launcher)
  for how hooks and the MCP server find one.
- `plugin.json` `version` is pinned to `package.json` by `check-pins`. A
  pinned version keeps users on it until the next release changes it.

Combining the plugin with a loose `install --harness claude-code` is safe
(one session identity, duplicate hooks dropped by the daemon, #54), but
registers two MCP servers; keep one. Once the plugin is enabled, re-running
`load-lock install --harness claude-code` (or `load-lock setup --yes`) moves
the loose MCP server, hooks and `CLAUDE.md` section out (`--legacy` keeps
them), and `load-lock doctor` reports the mode (`claudeCodeMode`: `plugin`,
`loose`, `both` or `none`) and warns on `both`.

### macOS seatbelt — contract-inspected

**No macOS machine was available** for this verification, so this is
contract-inspected against the `sandbox-exec(5)`/seatbelt documentation,
not executed here.

On macOS the daemon listens on a Unix domain socket at
`~/.local/state/load-lock/daemon.sock`, and connecting to a UDS is
mediated by seatbelt as a *file* operation, not a network one — so a
profile needs read and write access to the socket path, e.g.:

```lisp
(allow file-read-data
  (literal "/Users/you/.local/state/load-lock/daemon.sock"))
(allow file-write*
  (literal "/Users/you/.local/state/load-lock/daemon.sock"))
```

(no `network-outbound` rules required for the path-socket transport;
`allow network*` forms are not the mechanism a UDS connect goes through
under seatbelt). Since the socket inode is recreated when the daemon
restarts, allow the containing directory too if your profile is
path-literal strict, or re-generate the profile. Expected outcome
(unverified): with those file rules plus the env vars
(`LOAD_LOCK_SOCKET`, `LOAD_LOCK_NO_SPAWN=1`,
`LOAD_LOCK_LABEL_PREFIX=…`) passed through to the agent, a seatbelt-sandboxed
client talks to the host daemon exactly as in the verified bubblewrap
case. omac's macOS sandboxing uses seatbelt under the hood with the same
`environment.allow_vars` env-stripping as on Linux, so the omac installer
(`load-lock install --harness omac`, live-verified on Linux against omac
0.11.0 — see above) applies unchanged; only the socket path and the
seatbelt file rules differ.

### WSL2 — honest state

There is no verified cross-boundary story for WSL2, and we won't pretend
otherwise:

- The Windows transport is a named pipe (`\\.\pipe\load-lock`); named
  pipes are not reachable from inside a WSL2 distro. A WSL-side Unix
  socket is likewise not reachable from Windows-native processes.
- There is deliberately no TCP transport (a non-goal), so there is no
  loopback bridge to fake one.

The realistic shape: **the WSL2 Linux VM is the host.** Run the daemon
inside the distro (`~/.local/state/load-lock`, normal install — see the
WSL2 procedure subsection above for the unverified-but-expected resource
reporting), and treat Windows-native agents as out of scope for now.
Cross-distro bridging (two distros sharing one daemon via a `/mnt/wsl`
shared directory bind-mounted as the state dir) is an *unverified
expectation*: `/mnt/wsl` is shared across distros, so the same
bind-the-state-dir recipe should apply, but nobody has run it — verify
and record before relying on it. Keep the state dir on the Linux
filesystem, not `/mnt/c` (drvfs/9p is slow and lock semantics differ, as
in the WSL2 caveats above).

## macOS / Windows notes

- macOS: no cgroup limits; process-liveness checks fall back from
  `/proc/<pid>/stat` start times to `kill(pid, 0)` (weaker PID-reuse
  defense — document and prefer `run_with_permit`). Everything else works.

### Windows — procedure (NOT verified here)

**No Windows environment was available on the verification machine** (all
development and testing happened on Linux). The transport adapter is
implemented in `src/shared/transport.ts` and its logic is covered by
`src/test/platform.test.ts` (endpoint resolution, pipe naming, probe,
stale-cleanup, liveness, and job-tree kill paths, exercised via platform
injection on Linux) — but nothing in this subsection has been executed on
Windows. It is a ready-to-run procedure with *expected* outcomes, to be
verified and recorded by someone with a Windows setup.

What the adapter does:

- Transport: clients and the daemon talk over the named pipe
  `\\.\pipe\load-lock` (Node's `net` module accepts pipe paths in
  `connect`/`createServer` natively). No Unix-domain socket is involved.
- State dir: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\load-lock` (falls back to
  `%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\load-lock`); `LOAD_LOCK_STATE_DIR` and
  `LOAD_LOCK_SOCKET` overrides still win, as on POSIX.
- Daemon claim: a second daemon probes the pipe before listening and
  exits with "denied" if a live daemon answers (same semantics as the
  POSIX socket claim). Because a named pipe is a kernel object, there is
  no stale-socket file to clean up.

1. Install Node 20+ on Windows and install the package:

   ```powershell
   npm install -g @aron98/load-lock
   load-lock install --harness <harness>
   load-lock doctor
   ```

   Expected: `doctor` reports the `%LOCALAPPDATA%\load-lock` state dir and
   reaches the daemon over the pipe (it probes by connecting, since a pipe
   is not a filesystem entry).

2. Run two `load-lock acquire` in separate shells, then `load-lock dashboard --once`.

   Expected: the same queue/permit behavior as on Linux — the pipe carries
   the identical NDJSON protocol.

3. Start a permit-tracked job (`run_with_permit` / `load-lock run`), kill
   the job, and confirm the permit auto-releases via the sweep.

4. Run `load-lock service stop`, then any tool call.

   Expected: the daemon exits and the next client auto-spawns a fresh one.

Caveats to watch for (unverified expectations):

- **No PID-reuse defense.** Windows has no `/proc`-style start time, so
  `isProcessAlive` can only use `kill(pid, 0)` semantics. A recycled PID
  could be mistaken for the original job — the same limitation as macOS,
  documented here rather than solved.
- **No process-group scan.** The `/proc`-based process-group scan does not
  exist on Windows. Tracked permits release when the main PID dies even if
  child processes survive; job stop/kill uses `taskkill /PID <pid> /T`
  (`/F` for SIGKILL) to take down the tree.
- **Pipe name is machine-wide.** Unlike POSIX, where each user gets their
  own state dir and socket, a named pipe named `\\.\pipe\load-lock` is
  machine-global — two Windows users on one host share one daemon. Point
  `LOAD_LOCK_SOCKET` at a different pipe name if that is a problem.
- `inspect_machine` cgroup detection reads `/sys/fs/cgroup` and will
  degrade gracefully (`cgroupVersion: "none"`), reporting raw host numbers.

## Releasing (maintainers)

Publishing is automated: publishing a GitHub Release runs
`.github/workflows/publish.yml` (npm Trusted Publishing; read its comments
before changing the flow). The release commit itself is manual:

1. Bump `version` in `package.json` (and `package-lock.json`), e.g.
   `npm version 1.6.0 --no-git-tag-version`.
2. Sync every pinned `@aron98/load-lock@<version>` to it:
   `npm run check-pins -- --write` (alias for
   `node scripts/check-pins.mjs --write`), then `npm run check-pins` must
   print `pins ok`. Commit the bump and the pin updates together.
3. Merge, then publish a GitHub Release tagged `v<version>`.

Pinned files (the skill's npx fallback, ACE `ace/mcp/mcp.json` and
`ace/opencode/package.json`, the Claude Code plugin's `plugin.json` and
launcher) are declared in the
`PINNED` list at the top of `scripts/check-pins.mjs`; add an entry whenever
a new artifact pins a version. CI (`pins` job in `ci.yml`) fails on any
pin that differs from `package.json`, on a declared file that is missing,
and on a declared file that no longer contains a pin.
